waves.title: AFC East (BUF, MIA, NE, NYJ) & AFC North (BAL, CIN, CLE, PIT) Deep Tactical, Trench, Beat-Writer & Vulnerability Dossiers
waves.content:
This is a public-data dossier for the 2026 season, anchored to Sharp Football (updated Nov. 3), Muffed PROE through Week 8, and current coaching lists. It is not a betting card. Several items you asked for are not in any public chart I could verify, and those cells are marked rather than filled with guesses.

**Not publicly charted, so not invented here:** five-man protection rules, slide-direction maps, silent-count road grades, full Cover-0/1/2/3/4/6 splits for every team, simulated-creeper rates, individual YPRR and fantasy points per route allowed, exact inside-the-5 run/pass splits, and specific Wednesday-to-Friday practice or locker-room tells. Pace below is Sharp’s neutral play-clock seconds used (lower is faster), not snap-to-snap seconds. PROE is all-situation pass rate over expected, not a trailing-by-8 versus leading-by-8 split. That script split is not in the tables.

---

## Buffalo Bills

**1. Scheme and volume.** Head coach Joe Brady still calls the offense. Offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr. and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard are both in their first year in those seats. Brady’s offense is a heavy-tight-end outlier: 11 personnel 47%, 12 personnel 23%, 13 personnel 26%, 21 personnel 1%, 22 personnel 0%. Two-tight-end rate is 52%, among the league’s heaviest. PROE is −1.1 (neutral pass rate 51.8%). Neutral play-clock use is 32.5 seconds, near the league middle (average 32.7). Sharp did not publish a gear-change figure for Buffalo, so trailing-versus-leading elasticity is not in this cut. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Stated starters in recent rankings: Dion Dawkins, Alec Anderson, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence, Spencer Brown. The unit has graded as a top-tier run line. Dawkins surrendered six pressures in the Ravens game and still posted pass and run grades above 70. Protection rules, slide direction, and silent-count road vulnerability are not charted publicly. [[5]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-offensive-line-rankings-2026)

**3. Defense.** Leonhard has moved Buffalo toward two-high shells and more base. Through six weeks, Buffalo Rumblings charted the Bills first in Cover-4 (26%) and above average in Cover-3 (34.4%), so Cover-3 plus Cover-4 was over 60% of snaps. Week 1 dropback splits were Cover-0 0%, Cover-1 7%, Cover-2 12%, 2-Man 10%, Cover-3 31%, Cover-4 19%, Cover-6 21%. Season-long shell rates beyond man/zone are not fully published. Man rate 19.3%, zone 72.6%. Blitz rate 31.1%. Light box 40.2%, heavy box 32.4%, sub package 62%. Boundary corner Maxwell Hairston has been the coverage weak link: 36.4 PFF coverage grade (98th of 102 qualified corners) and a 114.6 passer rating allowed. YPRR is not in that report. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/) [[8]](https://athlonsports.com/nfl/buffalo-bills/bills-jim-leonhard-defense-penalties-ravens) [[9]](https://www.buffalorumblings.com/buffalo-bills-analysis/143309/buffalo-bills-defense-not-better-but-certainly-different-in-2026) [[10]](https://www.buffalorumblings.com/buffalo-bills-analysis/140185/buffalo-bills-jim-leonhard-coverage-diversity-something-to-watch-under-new-defensive-coordinator)

**4. Red zone.** Through Week 8, Sharp had Buffalo at 29 trips, 72% touchdown rate, 100% score rate, 46% pass rate inside the 20, and 89% goal-to-go touchdown rate. A separate goal-line grade through late October called Buffalo the league’s most run-heavy inside the 5, with Josh Allen and James Cook accounting for the goal-line rushes and 11 rushing scores already on the board. Tight-bunch rub rate is not charted. [[11]](https://fantasysixpack.net/2026-fantasy-football-goal-line-guide-week-8/) [[12]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-red-zone-stats/)

**5. Beat writers.** @JoeBuscaglia (The Athletic), @SalSports (Sal Capaccio, WGR), @JaySkurski, and ESPN’s Alaina Getzenberg. They are the participation and injury wire from Wednesday estimates through Friday. No verified practice-window “tell” beyond that reporting role should be treated as a signal.

**6. Situational edges that the data actually support.** Heavy 12/13 personnel is the structural tell: defenses that stay in nickel against three tight ends are playing Buffalo’s game. The defensive leak is boundary coverage, specifically Hairston, not a documented route family. Do not treat any single route concept as a proven prop edge without fresh charting.

---

## Miami Dolphins

**1. Scheme and volume.** First-year head coach Jeff Hafley. Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik calls plays (Shanahan tree). Defensive coordinator Sean Duggan is new. Personnel is the inverse of a spread pass offense: 11 personnel 58%, 12 personnel 9%, 13 personnel 0%, 21 personnel 28%, 22 personnel 3%. Two-back rate is 31%. PROE is league-worst at −10.7 (neutral pass rate 47.3%). Neutral play-clock use is 34.1 seconds, tied for fourth-slowest. Gear change +1.2, meaning the published trailing adjustment is small and in the slower direction on Sharp’s scale. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Public pass-block rankings have not isolated a single guard or tackle as a weekly 3-tech or wide-9 liability with a stable grade. Protection rules, slides, and silent counts are not charted.

**3. Defense.** Zone-heavy and passive up front. Man 17.0%, zone 74.8%, middle open 50.9%. Blitz rate 20.4%, second-lowest in this eight-team set. Light box 39.6%, heavy box 28.9%, sub package only 51%, so they are in base more than most. No verified slot or boundary weak link with YPRR. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

**4. Red zone.** Through Week 8: 17 trips, 59% touchdown rate, 34% pass rate inside the 20, 73% goal-to-go touchdown rate. The red-zone call sheet matches the season-long run lean. Inside-the-5 split and bunch-rub rate are not published. [[12]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-red-zone-stats/)

**5. Beat writers.** ESPN’s Marcel Louis-Jacques and @PoupartNFL. Use them for Wednesday participation, not for invented locker-room tells.

**6. Situational edges.** The offense is the most run-committed unit in the league on PROE, and it is slow. Unders and rush-volume props are the structural read, not a named route. On defense, the low blitz rate and high zone rate mean quarterbacks who can throw on time against two-high zone are not being stressed by extra rushers. That is a tendency, not a proven route list.

---

## New England Patriots

**1. Scheme and volume.** Head coach Mike Vrabel. Offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels calls plays. Defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr is new. Personnel: 11 personnel 60%, 12 personnel 24%, 13 personnel 3%, 21 personnel 9%, 22 personnel 5%. Two-back rate 14%. PROE −0.6 (neutral pass rate 49.8%), a slight run lean that can swing hard week to week (Muffed noted a −11.7 game against Miami). Neutral play-clock use 32.1 seconds, 11th-fastest. No published gear-change number. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Recent stated starters: Will Campbell, Walter Rouse, Jared Wilson, Matt Pryor, Morgan Moses. PFF flagged left guard as the weak spot, with Walter Rouse and Ben Brown both under 55.0 in the Miami game. That is the best public matchup note against interior rush. Slide rules and silent-count road data are not charted. [[5]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-offensive-line-rankings-2026)

**3. Defense.** Higher man and higher blitz than the rest of this set except the Jets. Man 29.0%, zone 65.7%. Blitz 37.8%. Light box 37.3%, heavy box 28.8%, sub package 77%. No verified individual YPRR weak link. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

**4. Red zone.** Team red-zone touchdown rate has sat in the low-to-mid 50s in season aggregates (about 54% in one board). Sharp’s full trip table for New England was not in the extract. Inside-the-5 split is not published. [[13]](https://nextlevelstats.com/leaderboards?view=teams&season=2026&category=drives&stat=rz_td&team=TB)

**5. Beat writers.** @MikeReiss (ESPN) and @ezlazar. Reiss remains the primary Wednesday-to-Friday injury and participation source.

**6. Situational edges.** Left guard is the trench leak against a 3-tech. On defense, the 37.8% blitz rate is the pressure tell: offenses that can identify the extra rusher and throw hot or to the checkdown are attacking the published tendency. No route concept has a verified “always beats New England” rate in the sources pulled.

---

## New York Jets

**1. Scheme and volume.** Head coach Aaron Glenn (second year, on the hot seat in November reporting). Offensive coordinator Frank Reich calls plays. Defensive coordinator Brian Duker is new. Personnel: 11 personnel 59%, 12 personnel 26%, 13 personnel 11%, 21 personnel 1%, 22 personnel 2%. PROE −2.4 (neutral pass rate 51.9%, overall pass rate 57.0%, so they throw more once script breaks). Neutral play-clock use 32.3 seconds. Gear change +0.2, almost no tempo change when trailing. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[14]](https://www.winnipegfreepress.com/sports/football/nfl/2026/11/06/several-coaches-on-the-hot-seat-need-major-turnarounds-in-the-second-half-to-keep-their-jobs) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Recent PFF look had Olu Fashanu, Jordan Meredith, Josh Myers, Joe Tippmann, and Armand Membou, with all five over 65 in one measured week and Tippmann the lowest pass-block grade of the group at 69.2 that week. Other boards have listed different guard pairings earlier in the year, so the interior is not stable enough to name a season-long 3-tech victim. Slides and silent counts are not charted. [[5]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-offensive-line-rankings-2026)

**3. Defense.** Most aggressive blitz rate in this set at 40.1%. Man 26.1%, zone 63.9%. Light box 41.1%, heavy box 28.7%, sub package 65%. No verified YPRR weak link. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

**4. Red zone.** Worst red-zone touchdown rate in one season board at 46%, and Sharp had them 32nd in EPA per red-zone play with a 57% pass rate inside the 20 and a 96% score rate. They reach the red zone and settle for threes. Inside-the-5 split is not published. [[13]](https://nextlevelstats.com/leaderboards?view=teams&season=2026&category=drives&stat=rz_td&team=TB) [[12]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-red-zone-stats/)

**5. Beat writers.** @RichCimini (ESPN). His November reporting has been on clock and timeout management, not on a coded practice tell. @BrianCoz remains a secondary local source from prior beat lists.

**6. Situational edges.** The published leaks are finishing drives (low red-zone touchdown rate) and a defense that blitzes on two of every five dropbacks. Hot routes and screens are the logical answer to that blitz rate. They are not a verified “this concept, this yardage” prop.

---

## Baltimore Ravens

**1. Scheme and volume.** First-year head coach Jesse Minter (Fangio/Harbaugh defensive tree). Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle calls plays. Defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver is new. Personnel still looks like a multiple-tight-end offense: 11 personnel 54%, 12 personnel 31%, 13 personnel 14%, 21 personnel 0%, 22 personnel 0%. Two-tight-end rate 45%. PROE −3.5 (neutral pass rate 51.9%). That run lean is partly quarterback-driven: scoring fell from 29.0 points per game in the first four weeks with Lamar Jackson to 15.8 without him. Neutral play-clock use 33.6 seconds, slow. No gear-change number. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[15]](https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-coordinator-rankings-midseason-packers-jonathan-gannon-steelers/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Not isolated to a single weak guard or tackle in the public rankings pulled. Slides and silent counts are not charted. Quarterback availability changes protection stress more than any published slide tendency.

**3. Defense.** Minter’s tree is two-high and light-box. The numbers match: man only 15.9%, zone 77.7%, middle open 59.5% (most open-middle rate in this set). Blitz 31.2%. Light box 51.7%, heavy box 19.1%, sub package 78%. No verified individual YPRR weak link. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

**4. Red zone.** About 59% touchdown rate on the season boards, middle of the league. Inside-the-5 split and bunch-rub rate are not published. [[13]](https://nextlevelstats.com/leaderboards?view=teams&season=2026&category=drives&stat=rz_td&team=TB)

**5. Beat writers.** @jeffzrebiec and @jamisonhensley. Jackson’s week-to-week status has been the only practice-window item that moves a number. Treat Friday designation as the tell, not midweek tone.

**6. Situational edges.** Split the offense by quarterback. With Jackson, the 12/13 personnel and designed quarterback run game are the card. Without him, the same personnel has produced a bottom-tier scoring offense. Against the defense, middle-open zone at 59.5% is the structural window for in-breakers. That is a shell tendency, not a named route with a verified yards-per-route figure.

---

## Cincinnati Bengals

**1. Scheme and volume.** Head coach Zac Taylor calls plays. Offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher. Defensive coordinator Al Golden (second year). Personnel is a 12-personnel offense: 11 personnel 48%, 12 personnel 43%, 13 personnel 2%, 21 personnel 4%, 22 personnel 0%. PROE is league-best at +7.9 (neutral pass rate 64.9%). Neutral play-clock use 34.1 seconds, slow, with gear change +1.1. They throw more than the situation expects, and they do it without speeding up. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Recent stated group: Orlando Brown Jr., Dylan Fairchild, Ted Karras, Dalton Risner, Amarius Mims. In the Titans overtime game, Brown accounted for six of ten pressures allowed, while Karras, Risner, and Mims all graded above 75 in pass protection, with Mims the highest-graded right tackle in that PFF cut. Left tackle versus a wide-9 is the public matchup, not a guard-versus-3-tech. Slides and silent counts are not charted. [[5]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-offensive-line-rankings-2026)

**3. Defense.** Most passive rush plan in this set. Blitz 19.1%. Light box 57.5%, the lightest box rate here. Man 28.5%, zone 64.0%. Sub package 82%. No verified YPRR weak link. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

**4. Red zone.** Among the better finishing offenses: about 68–70% touchdown rate depending on the board, and a passing goal-line grade that ranked at the top of one late-October sheet (five passing scores versus three rushing scores inside the 5 in that sample). Bunch-rub rate is not published. [[11]](https://fantasysixpack.net/2026-fantasy-football-goal-line-guide-week-8/) [[13]](https://nextlevelstats.com/leaderboards?view=teams&season=2026&category=drives&stat=rz_td&team=TB)

**5. Beat writers.** @pauldehnerjr and @Ben_Baby. Joe Burrow’s participation is the only midweek item that should move a price.

**6. Situational edges.** The offense will throw in 12 personnel more than the down-and-distance model expects. That is a pass-prop and opponent-rush-yard environment, not a specific route. On defense, a 19% blitz rate and a 57.5% light-box rate mean the run game is the structural attack if the box stays light. Confirm the box count on film before treating that as a bet.

---

## Cleveland Browns

**1. Scheme and volume.** First-year head coach Todd Monken calls plays. Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer (run-game background). Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg is new. Personnel is the spread outlier of this group: 11 personnel 74%, 12 personnel 13%, 13 personnel 0%, 21 personnel 7%, 22 personnel 7%. PROE +0.2 (neutral pass rate 54.5%). Neutral play-clock use 32.0 seconds, ninth-fastest. Gear change −0.3, essentially no script change. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Recent stated group in one ranking: Spencer Fano, Zion Johnson, Elgton Jenkins, Austin Barber, Tytus Howard. No stable public grade isolates a weekly 3-tech or wide-9 victim. Slides and silent counts are not charted. Quarterback (Watson protocol versus Shedeur Sanders in at least one November report) changes protection more than any published rule.

**3. Defense.** Most man-heavy defense in the league. Man 43.4%, zone 52.8%, middle closed 72.9%. Blitz 26.5%. Sub package 94%, so they almost never leave nickel or dime. Light box 37.0%, heavy box 27.2%. Rutenberg has kept an aggressive rush-and-cover identity and added coverage disguise. No verified individual YPRR weak link in the sources pulled. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/) [[16]](https://www.beaconjournal.com/story/sports/pro/browns/2026/08/07/mike-rutenberg-browns-defense/91211482007/)

**4. Red zone.** Poor finishing: about 45–47% touchdown rate, 56% pass rate inside the 20 in the Sharp extract, 78% goal-to-go touchdown rate. They are better once it is goal-to-go than on the full red-zone trip. Inside-the-5 split is not published. [[13]](https://nextlevelstats.com/leaderboards?view=teams&season=2026&category=drives&stat=rz_td&team=TB) [[12]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-red-zone-stats/)

**5. Beat writers.** @MaryKayCabot, @AkronJackson (Chris Easterling), and @DanielOyefusi. Quarterback designation is the Friday item that matters.

**6. Situational edges.** Man at 43% with the middle closed is the defensive identity. That is a win for quarterbacks who can win outside leverage and for backs who can punish light boxes in man, not a documented slot route that “always” beats a named corner. Offensively, 74% 11 personnel means the offense is not hiding extra blockers. Pressure props against this line are a film question, not a published slide tell.

---

## Pittsburgh Steelers

**1. Scheme and volume.** First-year head coach Mike McCarthy calls plays. Offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio is new. Defensive coordinator Patrick Graham is new and has been credited with a defensive rebound. Personnel: 11 personnel 63%, 12 personnel 25%, 13 personnel 3%, 21 personnel 5%, 22 personnel 2%. PROE +2.0 (neutral pass rate 61.3%). Neutral play-clock use 34.2 seconds, third-slowest in the league. Gear change +1.6, the largest trailing slowdown in this set. They throw more than expected and they do it slowly. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[2]](https://gridironexperts.com/nfl-coaches-list/) [[15]](https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-coordinator-rankings-midseason-packers-jonathan-gannon-steelers/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected)

**2. Offensive line.** Recent stated group: Troy Fautanu, Mason McCormick, Zach Frazier, Brock Hoffman, Max Iheanachor, after a Week 3 shuffle at right guard and right tackle. Frazier has been the standout, the only center in one PFF cut above 75 in both pass and run block. Early-season tackle concerns were the public weak side before the shuffle. Current 3-tech and wide-9 matchups are not stable enough to name a weekly victim. Slides and silent counts are not charted. [[5]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-offensive-line-rankings-2026)

**3. Defense.** Zone shell, low man. Man 12.6%, zone 81.9%, the highest zone rate in this set. Blitz 27.4%. Light box 48.5%, heavy box 23.8%, sub package 69%. Graham’s prior reputation is simulated pressure and creepers. The 2026 simulated-pressure rate is not in the Sharp table, so it is not stated here as a number. No verified YPRR weak link. [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

**4. Red zone.** Middling to poor: about 50–52% touchdown rate on season boards. One goal-line grade sheet had Pittsburgh as the most pass-leaning goal-line offense in that sample. Inside-the-5 split is not published as a raw run/pass percentage. [[11]](https://fantasysixpack.net/2026-fantasy-football-goal-line-guide-week-8/) [[13]](https://nextlevelstats.com/leaderboards?view=teams&season=2026&category=drives&stat=rz_td&team=TB)

**5. Beat writers.** @MarkKaboly and @Alex_Kozora. Aaron Rodgers participation is the Wednesday-to-Friday item. No coded practice tell beyond that.

**6. Situational edges.** Slow pace plus positive PROE is a pass-volume, low-play-count environment. On defense, 82% zone is the shell. In-breakers against zone are the logical concept family. They are not a verified yards-per-route number against a named slot or boundary corner.

---

## How to use this without lying to yourself

Personnel, PROE, neutral play-clock, man/zone, and blitz rate are the only cross-team numbers stable enough to compare this week. They come from Sharp’s Nov. 3 cut and Muffed’s Week 8 PROE board, and they will move. [[1]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-offensive-personnel/) [[3]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-team-pace-stats/) [[4]](https://muffed.ai/stats/pass-rate-over-expected) [[6]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-coverage-schemes/) [[7]](https://www.sharpfootballanalysis.com/stats-nfl/nfl-defensive-tendencies/)

The sharpest structural contrasts in this eight-team set:

- Pass identity: Cincinnati (+7.9 PROE, 43% 12 personnel) versus Miami (−10.7 PROE, 28% 21 personnel).
- Heavy personnel: Buffalo (26% 13 personnel) and Baltimore (45% two-tight-end) versus Cleveland (74% 11 personnel).
- Man versus zone: Cleveland (43.4% man, 94% sub) versus Pittsburgh (12.6% man, 81.9% zone) and Baltimore (middle open 59.5%).
- Blitz: Jets 40.1% and Patriots 37.8% versus Bengals 19.1% and Dolphins 20.4%.
- Pace: Patriots and Browns are the faster play-clock users. Steelers, Dolphins, Bengals, and Ravens are the slow group.

Anything more specific than that — a slide, a silent count, a creeper rate, a corner’s YPRR, a Friday practice quote treated as a market tell — needs a primary chart or the beat writer’s own post from that week. I will not supply those as if they were measured.

waves.title: AFC South (HOU, IND, JAX, TEN) & AFC West (DEN, KC, LV, LAC) Deep Tactical, Trench, Beat-Writer & Vulnerability Dossiers
waves.content:
I'll pull current scheme, personnel, protection, coverage, red-zone, and beat-writer data for all eight AFC South and AFC West teams. Starting with coaching identities and advanced tendency sources.

Coaching staffs shifted between the 2025 season and the current year. I’m pulling full-season charting and team-level scheme pages so the dossier stays tied to published numbers.

The public record does not support a fully measured dossier at the granularity you asked for. Slide rules, silent-count rates, simulated-creeper rates, player-level yards per route run, and an exact trailing-by-8 versus leading-by-8 script split are not in the open tables. Those cells are marked as not charted, not filled in. Numbers below are from Sharp Football’s November 3, 2026 update (about 14,851 league plays, roughly through Week 8–9), plus coaching lists current as of early November 2026. Partial-season rates will move.

Sharp’s pace figure is play-clock seconds used on a 40-second clock in neutral situations (first three quarters, within 14 points, excluding the final two minutes of the half), not traditional seconds between snaps. Gear change is how that clock changes when trailing, not an 8-point lead split. A dash means Sharp did not publish a gear-change value.

## Houston Texans

**1. Scheme and script.** DeMeco Ryans calls the defense. Nick Caley calls the offense. Matt Burke is the defensive coordinator. Caley is a Rams pass-game coordinator by background, so the identity is 11-personnel play-action with duo mixed in, not a pure gap or pure wide-zone offense. Ryans’ identity is nickel, light boxes, and more single-high zone than man.

2026 personnel on 423 plays: 11 at 66 percent, 12 at 20 percent, 13 at 9.5 percent, 21 and 22 at zero. PROE is +1.4. Neutral play-clock use is 32.8 seconds, with a 58.5 percent neutral pass rate. Gear change when trailing is not published. Motion is 56.0 percent, play-action 16.0 percent, average depth of target 9.1, shotgun 65.3 percent, no-huddle 5.6 percent. In 2025 the same staff was at 72.3 percent 11 personnel and 22.8 percent play-action, so the 2026 sample is a bit heavier and a bit less play-action than last year.

**2. Protection.** November 4 PFF lineup: Aireontae Ersery, Keylan Rutledge, Evan Brown, Ed Ingram, Trent Brown, ranked 31st. Footballguys had the same five around 27th in late October. Five-man slide direction and silent-count road rate are not charted in open data. The structural leak is the interior, not a proven blind-side collapse: Ingram has been the multi-year pressure problem at guard, which is the 3-technique matchup, while Ersery is still a young left tackle against wide-9 speed. Do not treat a specific slide call as known.

**3. Coverage.** 2026: man 15.5 percent, zone 80.5 percent, middle closed 58.2 percent, middle open 39.9 percent. Blitz rate 23.8. Light box 47.1, heavy box 22.4, sub package 79.0. That is a single-high, four-man, nickel profile, not a pressure defense. Creeper rate and full Cover-0/1/2/3/4/6 splits for 2026 are not in the free table. The 2025 NFL Savant shell mix under the same staff was Cover-1 29.1, Cover-3 22.8, Cover-2 22.5, Cover-4 12.1, Cover-6 7.2, with man at 32.1 percent. Man has been cut roughly in half in 2026, so do not carry the 2025 Cover-1 rate forward. Yards per target allowed: outside 10.1, slot 7.9, tight end 7.3, running back 3.6. The weak link is the boundary, not the slot. Player-level yards per route run is not in the open table.

**4. Red zone.** Inside-the-5 run/pass split, bunch-rub rate, and quarterback-sneak rate are not published for 2026. In 2025 Houston’s red-zone rush average was 2.03 yards on 77 carries, one of the worst marks in the league, and the passing red-zone sample was 74 attempts for 229 yards with no interceptions. That is a finishing problem, not a sneak-heavy identity.

**5. Beat writers.** Jonathan M. Alexander (@jonmalexander, Houston Chronicle) and DJ Bien-Aime (@Djbienaime, ESPN) are the practice-window accounts. Nick Schwager (@NickSchwagerNFL) is the local follow. I could not verify a standing Wednesday-to-Friday coded tell. What they actually post is participation (DNP, limited, full), which lineman is working with the ones, and whether Stroud is in the shotgun or under center in team periods. Read those posts live. Do not treat a recycled quote as a snap-count tell.

**6. Published leaks.** Attack the boundary, not the slot: 10.1 yards per target outside versus 7.9 in the slot. Running backs are not the matchup (3.6). The offensive leak is protection, specifically interior pressure into a quarterback who still pushes the ball downfield (9.1 aDOT). Props that assume a slot massacre or a pass-funnel against this defense are fighting the 2026 chart.

## Indianapolis Colts

**1. Scheme and script.** Shane Steichen calls the plays. Jim Bob Cooter is the offensive coordinator. Lou Anarumo calls the defense. Steichen’s identity is motion, 12 personnel, and run-pass options, with the quarterback as a runner. Anarumo’s identity is disguise and simulated pressure more than raw blitz volume. Pro Football Reference still tags the offense West Coast and the defense 4-3, which understates the motion rate.

2026 personnel on 514 plays: 11 at 58 percent, 12 at 32 percent, 13 at 10 percent, 21 and 22 at zero. PROE is −1.8. Neutral play clock 33.2 seconds, neutral pass rate 57.0 percent, gear change +0.1 (almost no tempo change when trailing). Motion 62.0 percent, play-action 16.4 percent, aDOT 7.0, shotgun 63.2 percent, no-huddle 4.0 percent. This is a deliberate, run-leaning, two-tight-end offense, not a no-huddle.

**2. Protection.** Quenton Nelson is out. PFF’s November 4 lineup was Bernhard Raimann, rookie Jalen Farmer, Tanor Bortolini, Matt Goncalves, Jalen Travis, ranked 15th that week after Farmer’s first start produced a 25.9 pass-blocking grade and three pressures. Footballguys had the same group near 30th on October 29. Slide rules and silent-count rate are not charted. The clearest 3-technique leak is Farmer at left guard. Raimann is the more stable tackle. Road silent-count stress is a reasonable inference for a rookie guard next to a young center, not a measured rate.

**3. Coverage.** Man 25.3 percent, zone 67.5 percent, middle closed 51.0 percent, middle open 43.6 percent. Blitz only 21.2, with a light-box rate of 37.7 (low for this group) and a heavy-box rate of 27.7. Sub package 66.0. Low actual blitz plus Anarumo’s history is the creeper profile, but 2026 creeper frequency is not published. Full shell splits are not in the free table. Yards per target: slot 10.5, running back 8.8, tight end 7.6, outside 7.0. The weak link is the slot and the backfield, not the boundary corner. Player yards per route run is not published.

**4. Red zone.** Through Weeks 1–7, Jonathan Taylor had 28 of 59 red-zone chances (47 percent) and 13 carries inside the 5. Daniel Jones had two goal-line runs in that window. That is a Taylor-inside-the-5 offense, not a sneak-or-bunch offense. A full inside-the-5 pass rate and a tight-bunch rate are not published.

**5. Beat writers.** Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) is the longest-tenured practice voice. Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen, ESPN) posts opponent-week context, not just Colts quotes. Destin Adams (@TheDestinAdams) is the draft-and-roster follow. The Wednesday tell that has actually shown up is offensive-line participation after Nelson’s absence: who is working at left guard in team periods, not a coded locker-room phrase.

**6. Published leaks.** Slot targets and running-back targets are the coverage bets the chart supports (10.5 and 8.8 yards per target). Outside receivers are the wrong side (7.0). On offense, the leak is Farmer in pass protection and a script that does not speed up when trailing (gear change +0.1, PROE −1.8). Live-ball unders are more coherent than “they will throw their way back” overs unless the score forces it.

## Jacksonville Jaguars

**1. Scheme and script.** Liam Coen calls the plays. Grant Udinski is the offensive coordinator. Anthony Campanile calls the defense. Coen is McVay-tree: under-center play-action, condensed splits, and a slow operation. Campanile’s 2025 identity was two-high and Cover-6 heavy.

2026 personnel on 406 plays: 11 at 60 percent, 12 at 27 percent, 13 at 12 percent, 21 and 22 at zero. PROE is −3.2. Neutral play clock 34.5 seconds, the slowest in the league, neutral pass rate 56.9 percent. Gear change is not published. Motion 60.1 percent, play-action 14.7 percent, aDOT 8.5, shotgun only 53.9 percent, no-huddle 3.4 percent. They stay under center and they do not hurry.

**2. Protection.** PFF’s November 4 five: Walker Little, Emmanuel Pregnon, Robert Hainsey, Ezra Cleveland, Cole Van Lanen, ranked 20th, with Cleveland limited by an ankle heading into a short week. Slide direction and silent-count rate are not charted. The matchup to watch is Cleveland at right guard against a 3-technique if he plays, and Van Lanen at right tackle against a wide-9 if Little is the stable side. That is a lineup inference, not a pressure-allowed split.

**3. Coverage.** Man 18.9 percent, zone 75.3 percent, middle closed 44.9 percent, middle open 52.2 percent. Blitz 26.1. Light box 47.5, heavy box 21.1, sub 73.0. Two-high lean, moderate blitz, light boxes. Creeper rate is not published. In Week 11 of 2025, Fantasy Points had Jacksonville at a league-high 22 percent Cover-6, 52 percent two-high, and 75 percent zone, while allowing the second-most schedule-adjusted points to tight ends and outside receivers and the fewest to the slot. 2026 yards per target flipped the tight-end side: tight ends 4.8 (best of these eight), outside 10.4, slot 9.2, running back 5.6. The 2026 weak link is the boundary, not the tight end. Do not reuse the 2025 tight-end funnel.

**4. Red zone.** 2026 inside-the-5 split is not published. In 2025 Jacksonville led these teams in red-zone rushing volume (110 carries, 327 yards, 15 touchdowns). That is a run-finish profile under Coen, not a documented sneak package.

**5. Beat writers.** Ryan O’Halloran (@ryanohalloran, Florida Times-Union) posts the division picture and availability. Demetrius Harvey (@Demetrius82) is the film-and-numbers local. Hays Carlyon (@HaysCarlyon) and John Shipley are the other practice-window accounts. Michael DiRocco is the ESPN Nation voice. The actionable Wednesday item this year has been Cleveland’s ankle and whether Little or Van Lanen is the right tackle in team periods. There is no verified coded locker-room tell.

**6. Published leaks.** Throw outside. 10.4 yards per target on the boundary, against a defense that plays middle-open more than middle-closed and does not blitz its way out of structure. Do not force tight ends (4.8). On the other side of the ball, this offense is the slowest neutral operation in the league and passes under expectation. Game totals that need a Jaguars tempo spike are betting against the chart.

## Tennessee Titans

**1. Scheme and script.** Robert Saleh is the head coach. Brian Daboll is the offensive coordinator and the play-caller. Gus Bradley is the defensive coordinator. Both Saleh and Bradley are Cover-3 coaches by career. Daboll’s identity is Erhardt-Perkins, shotgun, and no-huddle, not Shanahan wide zone.

2026 personnel on 449 plays: 11 at 78 percent (league high), 12 at 16 percent, 13 at 3.8 percent, 21 at 0.7 percent, 22 at 0.4 percent. PROE is −2.3. Neutral play clock 31.2 seconds, third-fastest in the league, neutral pass rate only 54.8 percent. Gear change +2.1, meaning they change tempo when trailing more than most of this group. Motion 47.6 percent, play-action 15.1 percent, aDOT 6.4 (short), shotgun 71.8 percent, no-huddle 20.0 percent (by far the highest of these eight). Fast, spread, short, and run-leaning in neutral.

**2. Protection.** Footballguys’ late-October five: Dan Moore, Peter Skoronski, Austin Schlottmann, Atonio Mafi, JC Latham. Through four games RotoWire had the unit at a 25.3 percent pressure rate (10th-lowest) and Latham at four pressures on 145 pass-blocking reps, while yards before contact sat 23rd. Slide rules and silent-count rate are not charted. The speed-rush side to test is Moore at left tackle, not Latham. Interior cohesion (Schlottmann and Mafi) is the run-game problem more than a proven 3-technique collapse. A 20 percent no-huddle rate in the gun raises silent-count exposure on the road, but that rate is not published.

**3. Coverage.** Man 16.8 percent, zone 77.0 percent, middle closed 47.2 percent, middle open 49.5 percent. Blitz 23.9. Light box 46.5, heavy box 23.4, sub 69.0. Balanced shells, not an extreme single-high or two-high team, despite the Saleh and Bradley Cover-3 reputations. Creeper rate and shell splits are not in the free table. Yards per target: slot 11.3, outside 9.2, running back 7.0, tight end 6.0. The weak link is the slot. Player yards per route run is not published.

**4. Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split, bunch rate, and sneak rate are not published for 2026. The offensive signature in the open data is 11 personnel and a short passing game, which usually means red-zone targets to the slot and the back rather than a tight-bunch rub package. That is an inference, not a charted call rate.

**5. Beat writers.** Turron Davenport (@TDavenport_NFL, ESPN) is the practice-window account. His posts this fall have been roster and development items (Cam Ward, Tony Pollard, Jeffery Simmons), not a coded injury tell. Read his Wednesday participation notes directly. There is no verified locker-room phrase that maps to a snap-count change.

**6. Published leaks.** Slot targets are the clean coverage number (11.3 yards per target) against a defense that does not play much man (16.8 percent). Tight ends are the wrong side (6.0). On offense, the no-huddle rate and the +2.1 gear change are the pace angle when they trail. Neutral PROE is still negative, so a trailing script is not the same thing as a neutral pass-heavy script.

## Denver Broncos

**1. Scheme and script.** Sean Payton is the head coach. Davis Webb is the offensive coordinator. Vance Joseph calls the defense. Gridiron Experts reported that Payton gave Webb the call sheet and took it back in October 2026. Edgehalla still listed Webb as the caller. Treat play-calling as Payton’s system with a midseason handoff dispute, not as a clean Webb offense. Joseph’s identity is pressure and more man than the rest of this division.

2026 personnel on 432 plays: 11 at 61 percent, 12 at 21 percent, 13 at 6.9 percent, 21 at 4.6 percent, 22 at 4.4 percent. PROE is −0.4. Neutral play clock 33.6 seconds (slow), neutral pass rate 59.1 percent, gear change +0.5. Motion 52.4 percent, play-action 15.4 percent, aDOT 5.6 (shortest of these eight), shotgun 64.0 percent, no-huddle 5.5 percent. Horizontal Payton offense, not a vertical one.

**2. Protection.** This is the best five in the group. PFF on November 4 ranked them 4th: Garett Bolles, Ben Powers, Luke Wattenberg, Quinn Meinerz, Mike McGlinchey, and cited one pressure allowed in the Chiefs game with every starter at 65.0 or better. Footballguys had them 1st. RotoWire noted Bolles on the hip injury list. Slide rules and silent-count rate are not charted. There is no clean 3-technique or wide-9 leak in the 2026 public grades. Bolles’ availability is the only structural watch. Payton’s historical protection is half-slide with the back as a check-down, but that is tree knowledge, not a 2026 call rate.

**3. Coverage.** Man 25.5 percent, the highest of these eight. Zone 69.6 percent. Middle closed 48.5 percent, middle open 47.6 percent. Blitz 34.7, also the highest of these eight. Light box 41.7, heavy box 29.3, sub package only 63.0. In the full 2025 season this defense had the league’s lowest zone rate at 55.0 percent, so the man-and-pressure identity is real and not a four-game blip. Creeper rate is not published. Joseph pressures more than he simulates. Yards per target: outside 7.6, slot 6.8, tight end 7.8, running back 6.7. There is no soft coverage landmark in this sample. Player yards per route run is not published.

**4. Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published for 2026. Payton’s career signature is the quarterback sneak and the screen near the goal line, and Bo Nix has a designed-run role. In 2025 Denver was one of the more run-tilted goal-line grades in early-season tracking, with a modest red-zone pass sample (81 attempts, 303 yards, one interception). Treat sneak usage as a Payton tendency, not a counted 2026 rate.

**5. Beat writers.** Nick Kosmider (@NickKosmider, The Athletic) is the cleanest Wednesday-to-Friday voice. Mike Klis (@mikeklis), Troy Renck (@TroyRenck), and Chris Tomasson (@christomasson) cover the same window. The tell that has actually mattered is Bolles’ hip participation and whether Payton or Webb is described as holding the call sheet after Wednesday. Kosmider’s recent posts have been game narrative and availability, not a coded phrase.

**6. Published leaks.** This defense is the wrong team to attack through air yards. Blitz rate is high, man rate is high, and both outside and slot yards per target are under 8. The offensive leak is horizontal volume at a slow pace (5.6 aDOT, 33.6-second neutral clock), so unders and rushing props fit the chart better than explosive-pass props. If Bolles sits, the wide-9 side becomes the first real protection crack. That is conditional, not current.

## Kansas City Chiefs

**1. Scheme and script.** Andy Reid calls the plays. Eric Bieniemy is back as offensive coordinator. Steve Spagnuolo calls the defense. Reid’s identity is West Coast motion, bunch, and a short passing game with selective shots. Spagnuolo’s identity is two-high simulated pressure. Bieniemy does not override Reid’s call sheet.

2026 personnel on 416 plays: 11 at 55 percent, 12 at 33 percent, 13 at 8 percent, 21 at 4 percent, 22 at zero. PROE is +4.9, fourth in the league. Neutral play clock 32.1 seconds, neutral pass rate 58.8 percent. Gear change is not published. Motion 53.5 percent, play-action 20.0 percent (highest of these eight), aDOT 5.7, shotgun 60.3 percent, no-huddle 0.7 percent. They pass over expectation without playing fast and without going no-huddle.

**2. Protection.** Footballguys’ late-October five: Kahlil Benson, Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey, Trey Smith, Jaylon Moore, ranked 11th. PFF still had the unit in the top tier in late October. Slide rules and silent-count rate are not charted. Humphrey and Smith are the stable interior. The speed-rush test is the tackle spot that is not a long-term blind-side fixture (Benson or Moore, depending on the week), not a 3-technique hunt at Smith. Reid’s historical answer to pressure is max protection and a back in the route, which fits a 5.7 aDOT. That is tree knowledge, not a 2026 slide chart.

**3. Coverage.** Man 16.5 percent, zone 79.7 percent, middle closed 44.5 percent, middle open 52.8 percent. Blitz 26.4. Light box 40.4, heavy box 26.0, sub 67.0. Two-high lean with a moderate blitz rate is consistent with Spagnuolo, but the 2026 creeper rate is not published. Do not quote an old simulated-pressure percentage as this year’s number. Yards per target: outside 7.5, slot 7.7, tight end 6.6, running back 7.1, wide receiver 6.9. No soft landmark. In 2025 the same defense was at 63.0 percent zone, so 2026 is more zone than last year, not more man.

**4. Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. Reid’s signature is the sneak, the shovel, and the bunch rub, and Mahomes’ sneak and rush usage is a career fact. 2025 red-zone passing was 80 attempts, 268 yards, three interceptions, alongside 87 rushes for 262 yards and 13 rushing touchdowns. That is a balanced finish, not a pass-only red zone. A 2026 sneak count is not in the open table.

**5. Beat writers.** Nate Taylor (@ByNateTaylor, ESPN) is the practice-window account. Jesse Newell (@jessenewell) and Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) cover availability and roster. The Wednesday item that changes a number is who is at left tackle and whether a receiver is limited, not a locker-room code. I could not verify a standing Friday tell beyond the injury report.

**6. Published leaks.** Coverage props against this defense are thin. Every alignment is in the 6.6 to 7.7 yards-per-target band. The offensive number that is actually extreme is PROE (+4.9) with almost no no-huddle (0.7 percent) and a short aDOT (5.7). Pass attempts can rise without pace or explosives rising. That is a volume profile, not a shot-play profile. Spagnuolo’s pressure is real, but the published blitz rate (26.4) is not an all-out rate, so “they live in Cover-0” is not supported.

## Las Vegas Raiders

**1. Scheme and script.** Klint Kubiak is the head coach and the play-caller. Andrew Janocko is the offensive coordinator. Rob Leonard is the defensive coordinator, and he is new, so 2025 Patrick Graham rates do not carry. Kubiak’s identity is Shanahan wide zone, heavy personnel, and play-action. The 2026 personnel table matches that identity more extremely than any other team in the league.

2026 personnel on 473 plays: 11 at 15 percent, 12 at 46 percent, 13 at 7.6 percent, 21 at 15 percent, 22 at 15 percent. Two-tight-end rate 70 percent. Two-back rate 30 percent. PROE is +0.6. Neutral play clock 31.7 seconds (fast for a heavy team), neutral pass rate 55.9 percent, gear change +2.4. Motion 60.6 percent, play-action 16.1 percent, aDOT 8.0, shotgun 54.5 percent, no-huddle 8.4 percent. They are heavy, they motion, and they speed up when trailing.

**2. Protection.** A full 2026 starter pressure split is not in the pages retrieved. Sharp’s June preview had the unit 25th and noted Ashton Jeanty contacted at or behind the line on 54 percent of carries in the prior year, second-worst in the league. Slide rules and silent-count rate are not charted. Kubiak’s tree uses reach blocks and tight-end chips more than a pure 5-man slide. The schematic stress is a wide-9 end setting the edge against a heavy, zone-run offense, and a 3-technique beating a guard on play-action. I will not name a 2026 “worst” guard without a pressure table.

**3. Coverage.** Man 21.0 percent, zone 70.7 percent, middle closed 46.0 percent, middle open 48.1 percent. Blitz 22.5, among the lower rates here. Light box 47.9, heavy box 29.5, sub 76.0. This is not a pressure defense in the published blitz rate. Creeper rate is not published, and Leonard’s shell preferences are not established enough to borrow from Graham. Yards per target: slot 11.4 (worst of these eight), wide receiver 9.3, running back 8.0, outside 8.8, tight end 6.5. The weak link is the slot and the backfield. Tight ends are covered. Player yards per route run is not published.

**4. Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. The personnel signature implies heavy red-zone looks (12, 21, 22) rather than empty 11. In 2025, under a different staff, red-zone rushing was poor (44 carries, 78 yards). Do not carry that Chip Kelly number onto Kubiak.

**5. Beat writers.** Paul Gutierrez (@PaulHGutierrez, ESPN) is the Nation voice. Vincent Bonsignore (@VinnyBonsignore) and Tashan Reed (@Tashanreed) cover the building. The beat has been thin relative to other clubs, which is itself a constraint: Wednesday participation posts are less dense, so do not invent a Friday tell that is not on the timeline. What matters when it is posted is which tight end is with the ones, because 70 percent of the offense is two-tight-end.

**6. Published leaks.** Slot and running-back targets are the coverage numbers (11.4 and 8.0). Tight ends are the trap (6.5) even though the offense you are watching uses tight ends constantly. On offense, the exploitable shape is heavy personnel into a light box, then play-action over the top (8.0 aDOT) once the defense adds a body. That is a schematic inference on top of a real personnel rate, not a route-win chart.

## Los Angeles Chargers

**1. Scheme and script.** Jim Harbaugh is the head coach. Mike McDaniel is the offensive coordinator. Chris O’Leary is the defensive coordinator, and he is new, so Jesse Minter’s 2025 Fangio rates do not carry. McDaniel’s Dolphins identity was 11 personnel, motion, and wide zone. The 2026 personnel table does not look like that. It looks like a Harbaugh fullback offense with McDaniel’s motion rate bolted on.

2026 personnel on 428 plays: 11 at 42 percent, 12 at 14 percent, 13 at 3 percent, 21 at 28 percent, 22 at 7 percent. Two-back rate 40 percent. PROE is −6.8, third-most run-heavy in the league. Neutral play clock 31.8 seconds, neutral pass rate 49.4 percent, gear change +0.9. Motion 62.8 percent (highest of these eight), play-action 18.4 percent, aDOT 7.1, shotgun 67.7 percent, no-huddle 5.6 percent. They motion like Miami and run like a Harbaugh team.

**2. Protection.** This is the clearest protection mess of the eight. RotoWire’s early-October account: Bradley Bozeman’s replacement path put Jake Slaughter at center after an ACL, Cole Strange was described as one of the worst guards in the league, Kayode Awosika and Trey Pipkins both struggled at left guard, and Rashawn Slater (high ankle), Joe Alt (neck), and Trevor Penning (concussion) were all out or limited around Week 4. Footballguys’ late-October five was Travis Burke, Awosika, Slaughter, Strange, Alt, ranked 24th. Pro Football Network had the unit in its bottom tier in late October, with run blocking ahead of pass blocking. Slide rules and silent-count rate are not charted. The 3-technique matchup is Strange. The wide-9 matchup is whichever tackle is not Alt or Slater that week. Road silent counts with a rookie or replacement center are a real operational risk. The rate is not published.

**3. Coverage.** Man 13.6 percent, second-lowest man rate in the league’s free table behind only a handful of teams. Zone 72.9 percent. Middle closed 41.9 percent, middle open 53.0 percent. Blitz 27.0. Light box 45.0, heavy box 30.7, sub 70.0. Two-high lean remains, but that is a 2026 O’Leary sample, not a Minter carryover. Creeper rate is not published. Yards per target: outside 9.2, tight end 8.7, slot 8.5, wide receiver 8.5, running back 4.4. The weak links are the boundary and the tight end. The backfield is covered. Player yards per route run is not published.

**4. Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. The personnel and PROE say the finish should be the second back and the quarterback run, not a 11-personnel rub menu. In 2025, under Greg Roman, red-zone passing was inefficient (81 attempts, 48.1 percent completions, 267 yards, four interceptions) while the offense was already multi-back. McDaniel has not flipped that into a pass-heavy red zone in the 2026 PROE. Sneak rate is not counted.

**5. Beat writers.** Daniel Popper (@danielrpopper, The Athletic) and Kris Rhim (@krisrhim1, ESPN) are the practice-window accounts. The Wednesday tell that has actually moved numbers is the tackle report: Slater, Alt, and Penning participation, plus who is at left guard. There is no verified coded locker-room phrase. If Popper or Rhim posts a non-starter at tackle on Wednesday, that is the tell. If they do not, do not infer one.

**6. Published leaks.** Throw to the boundary and to tight ends (9.2 and 8.7 yards per target) against a two-high, low-man defense. Do not build a receiving-back prop (4.4). On offense, the leak is protection, specifically Strange and the replacement tackle, into a run-heavy script that will not pass its way out of trouble unless the score forces the +0.9 gear change. Offensive explosive-pass props are betting against both the PROE and the line.

## What is shared, and what is not

Returning staffs are Houston, Indianapolis, Jacksonville, Denver’s defense, and Kansas City’s play-caller and defensive coordinator. Tennessee, Las Vegas, and the Chargers’ coordinator seats changed, so 2025 shell rates for those three defenses are the wrong prior. Houston’s own man rate fell from 32.1 percent in 2025 to 15.5 percent in 2026, which is a warning against copying last year’s Cover-1 share even when the names did not change.

The eight offenses are not one conference style. Tennessee is 78 percent 11 personnel. Las Vegas is 15 percent. The Chargers are 40 percent two-back and −6.8 PROE. Kansas City is +4.9 PROE with a 0.7 percent no-huddle rate. Jacksonville is the slowest neutral operation in the league. Denver is the shortest passing game. Those are the script facts. Protection slides, silent counts, creeper rates, and route-level yards per route run are not among them.

waves.title: NFC East (DAL, NYG, PHI, WAS) & NFC North (CHI, DET, GB, MIN) Deep Tactical, Trench, Beat-Writer & Vulnerability Dossiers
waves.content:
Public 2026 data can support a real dossier on scheme identity, personnel, pace, pass-rate lean, coverage family, and blitz. It cannot support invented protection rules, slide charts, silent-count splits, creeper rates, player-level yards per route run, or unpublished practice tells. Those cells are marked as not published. Figures below are regular-season aggregates through early November 2026 (about Week 8), so new coordinators are still small samples.

Sources for the numbers: Sharp Football personnel, PROE, pace, tendencies, blitz, man/zone, and positional yards per target, updated around November 3, 2026. Coaching identities match current staff lists. “Neutral pace” here is Sharp’s neutral-situation play-clock usage (seconds of the 40-second clock), not snap-to-snap seconds. League neutral average is 32.7. PROE is pass rate over expected in percentage points.

## How to read the gaps

Five-man protection rules, slide direction, 3-tech versus wide-9 matchup grades, and silent-count road splits are film and premium-grade items (PFF, SIS). They are not in the public tables. Coverage shell splits (Cover-0, Cover-1, Cover-2, Cover-3, Quarters, Cover-6) are not fully published for 2026 in one open table. What is published is man rate, zone rate, middle-closed, and middle-open. Simulated-creeper frequency is not separately published. Script elasticity when trailing by 8 or more versus leading by 8 or more is a filter on paywalled play-by-play, not a published team split. Beat-writer “tells” below are the windows those reporters actually cover. Specific unpublished Wednesday-Friday quotes are not invented here.

Betting notes are inferences from published splits, not certified route beaters.

## NFC East

### Dallas Cowboys

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Brian Schottenheimer calls the offense. Offensive coordinator Klayton Adams comes from an offensive-line and run-game background (Arizona). Defensive coordinator Christian Parker is new in 2026, hired from the Eagles’ defensive backs and pass-game staff under Vic Fangio. Expect a West Coast, play-action, outside-zone lean on offense, and a Fangio-influenced secondary on defense. Early 2026 numbers do not look like pure Fangio: more man and more middle-closed than Philadelphia.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 69%, 12 personnel 17%, 13 personnel 3%, 21 personnel 7%, 22 personnel 3% (511 plays). PROE +4.4, fifth in the league. Neutral play-clock 30.7, second-fastest. Motion 44.1%, play-action 15.6%, shotgun 64.3%, no-huddle 8.6%. Script elasticity by an 8-point margin is not published.

**Offensive line.** Slide rules, silent-count road rate, and a graded weakest guard or tackle versus 3-tech or wide-9 are not in open data. Do not treat any specific lineman as the confirmed weak link without a current pass-block grade.

**Defense.** Blitz rate 22.1%, light-box 50.4%. Man 23.3%, zone 67.7%, middle-closed 59.2%, middle-open 36.4%. Shell-by-shell rates and creeper rate are not published. Positional yards per target allowed: wide receiver 8.8, tight end 7.5, running back 5.1, outside 7.5, slot 11.5. The slot number is the soft spot in this division’s public data.

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 run/pass split and bunch-rub rate are not published for 2026. Schottenheimer’s history is situational passing near the goal line rather than a Philadelphia-style sneak identity. Quarterback-sneak volume is not a published signature.

**Beat writers.** @jonmachota (The Athletic) and @toddarcher (ESPN) are the sharpest daily voices. They post from The Star on open practice windows, Wednesday injury estimates, and Friday designations. Their usable tells are participation and target-share comments from Jerry Jones and the coordinators, not locker-room scheme leaks.

**Situational edge.** Attack the slot, not the boundary. Dallas allows 11.5 yards per target to the slot against 7.5 outside. That is the cleanest public matchup tell on this defense. Tempo also matters: Dallas snaps fast and passes over expectation, so live unders are fighting pace unless the game script flips.

### New York Giants

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach John Harbaugh is new in 2026. Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy is new, from the Reid tree in Kansas City. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson is new, from the Titans, in the Ravens-style disguise tree. Expect play-action and condensed looks in theory. Early 2026 reality is different: motion is only 36.5% (lowest of these eight) and play-action is 12.3%. Defense should be disguise-heavy with simulated pressure. Early blitz rate is high.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 42%, 12 personnel 19%, 13 personnel 2%, 21 personnel 15%, 22 personnel 18%. Two-back rate is 37%, an outlier. PROE −3.6. Neutral play-clock 34.0, slow. Shotgun 61.6%, air yards per attempt 9.1, no-huddle 8.6%. Script split by 8 points is not published. The offense is heavy, slow, and run-over-expected, with a vertical air-yards lean when it does throw.

**Offensive line.** Protection rules, slide tendency, and silent-count road vulnerability are not published. Heavy 21 and 22 personnel usually means more max-protect and chip help, which is a formation tell, not a confirmed slide chart.

**Defense.** Blitz 38.8%, light-box 40.8%, heavy-box 34.3%. Man 26.1%, zone 68.6%, middle-closed 49.2%, middle-open 47.5%. Creeper rate is not split out. Yards per target allowed: wide receiver 6.9, tight end 5.5, running back 5.8, outside 7.9, slot 5.7. This is one of the tighter coverage profiles in the group on published yards per target.

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. Heavy 21 and 22 personnel is the formation tell near the goal line. Quarterback sneak is not a published Giants signature under this staff.

**Beat writers.** @JordanRaanan (ESPN), @DDuggan21 (The Athletic), and @NYPost_Schwartz. Wednesday estimate and Friday designation posts are the practice-window product. Harbaugh’s first year has not produced a reliable public “install leak” pattern.

**Situational edge.** Do not build a prop card on “this defense is soft.” Published yards per target are low at tight end and slot. The offensive tell is the opposite: two-back volume and negative PROE. Live run props and under pace are more coherent than forcing a coverage beat that the yards-per-target table does not support. If Wilson’s simulated pressure shows up as the 38.8% blitz, hot routes and sight adjustments are the conceptual answer. Specific route trees that “always” win are not in the public data.

### Philadelphia Eagles

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Nick Sirianni. Offensive coordinator Sean Mannion is new in 2026, from the Packers quarterback room. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio remains. Fangio’s identity is two-high disguise, quarters and Cover-6 family, and a low true-blitz rate, with closed-post rotations (Cover-3 and Cover-1) spun out of an open look. A 2026 scheme note put Philadelphia near 87% two-high disguise and described the call menu as Cover-3, quarters/Cover-6, and Cover-1. Early 2026 aggregate rates: man 17.4%, zone 73.1%, middle-closed 51.3%, middle-open 41.6%, blitz 25.2%.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 77%, 12 personnel 20%, 13 personnel 3%, 21 and 22 essentially unused (476 plays). Second-highest 11 rate in the league. PROE +0.7, near neutral. Neutral play-clock 33.4, slower than the raw clock (31.5) because of a +3.2 gear change. Motion 54.2%, play-action only 10.8% (lowest of these eight), shotgun 71.9%, no-huddle 16.0% (highest of these eight). Script elasticity by 8 points is not published. The no-huddle rate is the elasticity clue: they speed up, they do not flip into a pass-only identity on the season PROE.

**Offensive line.** Slide rules and silent-count road splits are not published. The Brotherly Shove still depends on center-quarterback timing and a tight surface. That is a protection and snap issue, not a 3-tech slide chart.

**Defense.** Light-box rate on the tendencies page is high relative to blitz. Positional yards per target: wide receiver 8.5, tight end 7.1, running back 4.1, outside 9.3, slot 8.6. Boundary is softer than the slot on this table. Creeper frequency is not published. Fangio units usually simulate more than they send.

**Red zone.** The signature remains the quarterback sneak, the tush push. PFF’s multi-year count had Philadelphia at 163 sneaks over four seasons, with first-down conversion falling from 88.1% in 2022 to 83.7% in 2023, 77.6% in 2024, and 65.5% in 2025. Late-2025 failures against Detroit and Chicago are on film. Inside-the-5 run/pass split for 2026 is not published. Tight-bunch rubs are a secondary red-zone tool, not the signature. Mannion has not publicly retired the sneak. Sirianni still owns that call.

**Beat writers.** @ZBerm (The Athletic), @Jeff_McLane, and @BKubena. Wednesday injury and Friday inactive windows are the useful posts. Scheme tells come from Sirianni’s Monday transcript more than from closed practices.

**Situational edge.** Outside routes into a light box and a disguised single-high rotation are the structural idea, matching 9.3 outside yards per target. Do not treat the sneak as automatic. A 2025 conversion rate in the mid-60s is a live under on “Eagles convert short yardage,” not a lock. Running backs are a poor prop target against this defense (4.1 yards per target).

### Washington Commanders

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Dan Quinn. Offensive coordinator David Blough is new, promoted from the quarterback room after Kliff Kingsbury. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones is new, from the Vikings defensive backs and pass-game staff under Brian Flores. Expect a Flores-influenced simulated-pressure menu. Early blitz rate supports that: 40.3%, second on Sharp’s table.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 64%, 12 personnel 22%, 13 personnel 11%, 21 personnel 1%, 22 unused. PROE −1.1. Neutral play-clock 32.5. Motion 46.3%, play-action 15.8%, shotgun 71.9%, air yards 8.5, no-huddle 8.2%. Script split by 8 points is not published. Shotgun plus above-average air yards with a slightly negative PROE reads as vertical when they throw, not as a pass-happy script.

**Offensive line.** Protection rules, slide side, and silent-count road rate are not published. 13 personnel at 11% implies more six- and seven-man surfaces on early downs. That is a formation tell only.

**Defense.** Light-box 40.3%, heavy-box 23.8%, sub-package 54%. Man only 12.2%, zone 78.4%, middle-closed 32.1%, middle-open 61.0%. That is a two-high, high-blitz profile, consistent with a Flores pupil, but shell-by-shell and creeper rates are not published. Yards per target: wide receiver 7.8, tight end 9.4, running back 5.1, outside 9.1, slot 6.6. Tight end is the published soft spot. Slot is not.

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split and sneak rate are not published. 13 personnel is the heavy-package clue. No public sneak identity comparable to Philadelphia.

**Beat writers.** @john_keim (ESPN) remains the primary practice-window voice, with @NickiJhabvala on roster and injury. Wednesday estimates and Friday designations are the tells. Jones is new. There is no multi-year pattern of him tipping shells in open periods.

**Situational edge.** Tight end targets, especially intermediate crossers and seams against a middle-open, high-blitz shell, match the 9.4 tight-end yards per target. Slot props are the wrong side of the table (6.6). Blitz rate at 40% supports quick-game and hot-route concepts in theory. Exact route names that “consistently” win are not published.

## NFC North

### Chicago Bears

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Ben Johnson calls the offense. Offensive coordinator Press Taylor is the passing-game coordinator title, not an independent play-caller. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, in his second year, is a pressure and man-leaning coordinator relative to this group. Johnson’s identity, carried from Detroit, is motion, play-action, condensed splits, and multiple tight ends. Early 2026 confirms the personnel and the play-action, not a pure 11-personnel spread.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 48%, 12 personnel 34%, 13 personnel 17%, 21 and 22 unused. Two-plus tight end rate 51%, among the league’s heaviest. PROE +0.5. Neutral play-clock 31.6, fast. Motion 47.0%, play-action 20.0%, shotgun 52.9%, air yards only 6.3 (shortest of these eight), no-huddle 5.2%. Script elasticity by 8 points is not published. This is a fast, play-action, under-center-capable offense that throws short of the sticks in air yards, not a vertical PROE outlier.

**Offensive line.** Slide rules and silent-count vulnerability are not published. Heavy 12 and 13 personnel usually means tight end chips and slide protections to the passing strength. That is scheme logic, not a confirmed weekly slide chart or a named weak guard.

**Defense.** Blitz 34.6%. Man 29.5% (highest of these eight), zone 66.6%, middle-closed 52.5%, middle-open 43.3%. Creeper rate is not published. Allen’s units are more man and more five-man pressure than Fangio or Gannon. Yards per target: wide receiver 9.2, tight end 8.2, running back 6.5, outside 11.0, slot 7.4. Boundary is the published hole. Running-back yards per target allowed (6.5) is also the highest of these eight.

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. 13 personnel at 17% is the goal-line formation tell. Johnson’s Detroit red-zone menu used tight end leak and orbit motion more than quarterback sneak. Sneak rate under this Bears staff is not published.

**Beat writers.** @adamjahns and @kfishbain (The Athletic), @BradBiggs (Chicago Tribune). Wednesday participation and Friday injury designations are the window. Johnson does not tip play-calls in open viewing. The useful note is who is rotating at tight end, because 12 and 13 volume makes the third tight end a snap-share prop.

**Situational edge.** Boundary wide receiver, not slot. Outside yards per target allowed is 11.0 against 7.4 in the slot. Play-action at 20% with heavy personnel is the offensive tell for opponent defenses: light boxes get stressed, and the pass is often a shot off the run fake even when air yards stay short on the season average. Backfield targets are a secondary prop angle given 6.5 yards per target allowed.

### Detroit Lions

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Dan Campbell. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is new, from Arizona, a 12-personnel, play-action coordinator. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is in year two after the Glenn departure. Petzing’s early sample matches the résumé: 12 personnel 37% and play-action 20.2%, tied for the high end of these eight, with shotgun only 46.6%.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 53%, 12 personnel 37%, 13 personnel 7%, 21 personnel 3%, 22 unused. PROE 0.0. Neutral play-clock 31.6, fast, with a +2.5 gear change. Motion 50.4%, air yards 7.9, no-huddle 5.6%. Script split by 8 points is not published. Campbell’s fourth-down aggression is the real script elasticity, and it is not captured by PROE.

**Offensive line.** Slide rules, silent-count road rate, and a named weak tackle versus wide-9 are not in the open tables. Petzing’s 12-personnel offense typically uses tight end help to the slide side. That is a tendency class, not a weekly rule sheet.

**Defense.** Blitz 22.4%, light-box 47.3%, heavy-box 28.9%, sub-package only 54%. Man 18.1%, zone 76.8%, middle-closed 48.0%, middle-open 48.9%. Balanced post safety, low blitz. Creeper rate is not published. Yards per target: wide receiver 8.1, tight end 8.6, running back 4.4, outside 7.7, slot 9.1. Slot and tight end are the softer published surfaces. Running backs are not.

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. Campbell’s signature has been fourth-down goes and jumbo surfaces, not a tush-push monopoly. Sheppard’s short-yardage defense graded among the league’s best in 2025 on PFF’s sneak study, including stops of Philadelphia. That is a defensive red-zone note, not an offensive play-call rate.

**Beat writers.** @davebirkett (Detroit Free Press), @colton_pouncy (The Athletic), @Justin_Rogers, @ttwentyman. Wednesday injury and Friday practice notes are the window. Campbell’s Monday podium is more informative than closed-period leaks.

**Situational edge.** Slot and tight end, not running-back targets. A middle-of-the-field that is essentially split, with a modest blitz rate, is a better match for option routes and seams than for “they always bring pressure.” Opponent pace should expect a fast Detroit offense that does not pass over expectation. Unders need a grind, not a pass-funnel script.

### Green Bay Packers

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Matt LaFleur calls the offense. Offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich runs the run game from an offensive-line background. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is new in 2026, from Arizona. LaFleur’s tree is Shanahan: outside zone, wide zone, boot, and a 11/12/13 mix with almost no two-back. Gannon’s Cardinals and late Eagles tenure were quarters-heavy and low on coverage busts. Early 2026 Green Bay coverage fits a two-high coordinator: man 12.4%, zone 79.2%, middle-open 63.9%, middle-closed 31.5%.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 63%, 12 personnel 25%, 13 personnel 11%, 21 and 22 unused. PROE +6.5, second in the league. That is a real shift from the run-over-expected LaFleur profile of prior years. Neutral play-clock 32.7, league average. Motion 52.4%, play-action only 13.9%, shotgun 69.2%, air yards 9.2 (highest of these eight), no-huddle 7.9%. Script elasticity by 8 points is not published. The season already shows a pass lean that does not need a trailing script to appear.

**Offensive line.** Stenavich’s protections are a known coaching point in Packers film circles, but slide direction, silent-count road rate, and a graded weak guard versus 3-tech are not in the public aggregate. Do not name a lineman as the weak link from this dossier.

**Defense.** Blitz 31.2% on the November tendencies table, higher than Hafley’s late-career low-blitz profile. Gannon historically simulated more than he sent. Creeper rate is not split out. Yards per target: wide receiver 7.0, tight end 5.8, running back 5.8, outside 8.1, slot 4.9. Slot is a strength. Boundary is the relative soft side, and it is still not a collapse number.

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. 13 personnel at 11% is the heavy tell. LaFleur’s goal-line history is outside-zone and boot-action, with quarterback sneak used as a short-yardage tool rather than a Philadelphia-volume identity. 2026 sneak rate is not published.

**Beat writers.** @RobDemovsky (ESPN), @TomSilverstein (Milwaukee Journal Sentinel), @mattschneidman (The Athletic). Wednesday estimate and Friday practice-window posts are the product. Gannon is new. There is no established “he shows the shell on Wednesday” tell.

**Situational edge.** Do not bet the slot against Green Bay (4.9 yards per target). If you attack the coverage, it is the boundary against a middle-open quarters look, and the edge is modest. The offensive betting tell is PROE: Green Bay is passing more than the model expects, with the highest air yards of this group. Live unders against Green Bay need a lead and a clock, because the neutral pass rate is already elevated.

### Minnesota Vikings

**Staff and scheme.** Head coach Kevin O’Connell. Offensive coordinator Wes Phillips, McVay tree, in place since 2022. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Flores is the simulated-pressure and split-safety blitz reference point in the league. In 2024 Minnesota blitzed out of split-safety on 33.1% of plays. In 2025 that split-safety blitz rate was 37.4%. Early 2026 Sharp blitz rate is 69.8%, the league high on that table, with man at 5.4% and zone at 86.5%. Treat 69.8% as a published early-season figure under Sharp’s blitz definition, which folds in simulated pressure. It will not match every site’s “five or more rushers” number.

**Personnel, PROE, pace.** 11 personnel 58%, 12 personnel 19%, 13 unused, 21 personnel 13%, 22 personnel 7%. Two-back rate 22%. PROE −2.4. Neutral play-clock 34.4, slowest of these eight and last in the league on Sharp’s table. Motion 52.1%, play-action 18.9%, shotgun 58.6%, air yards 7.6, no-huddle 5.3%. Script split by 8 points is not published. This is a slow, slightly run-over-expected offense with real play-action, not a track meet.

**Offensive line.** Protection rules and silent-count road splits are not published. A Flores-style opponent increases the value of slide-and-scan and of “big on big” rules against simulated creepers. That is the conceptual vulnerability. The specific slide side and the weakest guard are not in open data.

**Defense.** Light-box 22.1%, heavy-box 38.2%, sub-package only 35% on the tendencies page. Middle-open 63.4%, middle-closed 29.4%. Shell-by-shell 2026 rates are not in the open table. The identity is two-high, zone, and pressure disguise. Yards per target: wide receiver 7.4, tight end 6.2, running back 3.9, outside 7.7, slot 7.1. Nothing on this table is a collapse. Running-back targets are a bad prop (3.9).

**Red zone.** Inside-the-5 split is not published. Two-back volume (21 and 22) is the formation clue. O’Connell’s red-zone history is motion and tight end isolated looks more than quarterback sneak volume. Sneak rate is not published.

**Beat writers.** @BenGoessling (The Athletic / Star Tribune), @alec_lewis, @CourtneyRCronin (ESPN). Wednesday participation and Friday designations are the window. Flores does not tip pressure packages in open viewing. The useful beat note is offensive-line availability, because the pressure menu punishes a backup guard.

**Situational edge.** The exploit is procedural, not a magic route. Simulated pressure and a two-high shell are beaten by formationing the protection (tight end or back to the creeper side), throwing hot on the green dog, and taking glance or choice routes behind dropping linemen. That is the concept class. It is not a published “this slot receiver at Y yards per route” stat. Avoid running-back receiving props. Avoid pace overs: Minnesota is the slowest neutral offense in the league on this table, with negative PROE.

## Cross-division card, public data only

| Team | 11 / 12 / 13 / 21 / 22 | PROE | Neutral clock | Blitz | Man / zone | Softest published surface |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DAL | 69 / 17 / 3 / 7 / 3 | +4.4 | 30.7 | 22.1 | 23.3 / 67.7 | Slot 11.5 YPT |
| NYG | 42 / 19 / 2 / 15 / 18 | −3.6 | 34.0 | 38.8 | 26.1 / 68.6 | No soft surface; outside 7.9 is least tight |
| PHI | 77 / 20 / 3 / 0 / 0 | +0.7 | 33.4 | 25.2 | 17.4 / 73.1 | Outside 9.3 YPT |
| WAS | 64 / 22 / 11 / 1 / 0 | −1.1 | 32.5 | 40.3 | 12.2 / 78.4 | Tight end 9.4 YPT |
| CHI | 48 / 34 / 17 / 0 / 0 | +0.5 | 31.6 | 34.6 | 29.5 / 66.6 | Outside 11.0 YPT |
| DET | 53 / 37 / 7 / 3 / 0 | 0.0 | 31.6 | 22.4 | 18.1 / 76.8 | Slot 9.1, tight end 8.6 |
| GB | 63 / 25 / 11 / 0 / 0 | +6.5 | 32.7 | 31.2 | 12.4 / 79.2 | Outside 8.1; slot is a strength at 4.9 |
| MIN | 58 / 19 / 0 / 13 / 7 | −2.4 | 34.4 | 69.8 | 5.4 / 86.5 | No soft surface; pressure is the issue, not YPT |

Fast and pass-leaning: Dallas and Green Bay. Fast and balanced: Chicago and Detroit, both in heavy personnel with 20% play-action. Slow and run-leaning: Giants and Vikings. Philadelphia is 11-personnel and no-huddle, not pass-over-expected. Washington is the tight-end coverage leak plus a Flores-style blitz rate. Chicago is the boundary coverage leak plus the heaviest tight-end offense in the group.

Anything more specific than that — a named guard’s slide, a corner’s yards per route run, a Wednesday install tell, or a route that “always” beats a coverage — would be fabricated. Those belong in a film account or a premium database, not in a filled-in blank.
